items.subject: eng

skill.th: การรับข้อเสนออย่างสุภาพ

topic.th: บทสนทนา: การตอบโต้ในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
Choose the most appropriate response to complete the conversation.
A: Would you like me to give you a lift to the station?
B: ______ I'd hate to take you out of your way.
A: It's no trouble — I'm heading that way anyway.

explanation.en: B is grateful but worried about inconveniencing A, and A reassures B. 'That's kind of you, but are you sure?' fits both. 'No, I wouldn't like that at all' is rude, 'I'll give you one too' misunderstands the offer, and 'I'm heading that way too' does not lead to A's reassurance.
explanation.th: B รู้สึกขอบคุณแต่เกรงใจว่าจะทำให้ A ต้องอ้อม และ A ก็ยืนยันว่าไม่ลำบาก That's kind of you, but are you sure? จึงเหมาะที่สุด ส่วน No, I wouldn't like that at all ไม่สุภาพ I'll give you one too เข้าใจข้อเสนอผิด และ I'm heading that way too ไม่สอดคล้องกับคำตอบของ A

choices: No, I wouldn't like that at all.
Don't bother — I'm heading that way too.
That's kind of you, but are you sure?
Yes, I'll give you one too.

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Making a suggestion that fits the reply
skill.th: การเสนอแนะให้สอดคล้องกับคำตอบ

topic.th: บทสนทนา: การตอบโต้ในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
Choose the most appropriate response to complete the conversation.
A: Have you finished the group report?
B: Not quite. Ton was supposed to write the conclusion, but he's been ill.
A: ______
B: I'd rather not. It's his section, and he said he'd send it tonight.

explanation.en: B's answer 'I'd rather not' must reply to a suggestion, and the reason ('It's his section') shows the suggestion was to write Ton's part: 'Should we write it ourselves, then?' The other questions cannot be answered with 'I'd rather not'.
explanation.th: คำตอบ I'd rather not ต้องตอบข้อเสนอ และเหตุผล It's his section แสดงว่าข้อเสนอคือการเขียนส่วนของต้นแทน จึงเป็น Should we write it ourselves, then? ส่วนคำถามอื่นตอบด้วย I'd rather not ไม่ได้

choices: Should we write it ourselves, then?
Why didn't you tell me sooner?
Has he sent it to you already?

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การตอบด้วยความสงสัยแบบแห้ง ๆ

topic.th: บทสนทนา: ความหมายแฝง

items.stem:
Choose the most appropriate response to complete the conversation.
A: I can't believe you told Mr Somsak his lesson was boring!
B: I didn't say "boring". I said it was "a bit slow".
A: ______

explanation.en: A doubts that B's softer wording changes anything: 'I'm not sure he'll see much difference.' 'Then he must have been delighted' and 'he loves criticism' are illogical, and 'So you did say it was boring' contradicts what B has just said.
explanation.th: A สงสัยว่าการเปลี่ยนคำให้นุ่มลงจะไม่ได้ช่วยอะไร จึงพูดว่า I'm not sure he'll see much difference ส่วน Then he must have been delighted และ he loves criticism ไม่สมเหตุสมผล และ So you did say it was boring ขัดกับที่ B เพิ่งพูด

choices: Then he must have been delighted.
I'm not sure he'll see much difference.
So you did say it was boring.
Oh, that's all right, then — he loves criticism.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การตีความคำตอบอ้อม ๆ

topic.th: บทสนทนา: ความหมายแฝง

items.stem:
Choose the most appropriate response to complete the conversation.
A: How was the job interview?
B: Put it this way: I don't think I'll be buying a new suit for my first day.
A: ______

explanation.en: B indirectly says there will be no first day, meaning the interview went badly. A sympathises: 'I'm sorry it didn't go well.' The other replies take B's words literally and miss the implication.
explanation.th: B บอกอ้อม ๆ ว่าคงไม่มีวันแรกของการทำงาน แปลว่าสัมภาษณ์ไม่ดี A จึงแสดงความเห็นใจว่า I'm sorry it didn't go well ส่วนคำตอบอื่นตีความตามตัวอักษรและพลาดความหมายแฝง

choices: Why don't you buy one anyway?
Oh no — I'm sorry it didn't go well.
So they gave you a uniform instead?

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การจับนัยที่อาจเป็นการดูถูก

topic.th: บทสนทนา: ความหมายแฝง

items.stem:
Choose the most appropriate response to complete the conversation.
A: Our presentation was chosen as the best in the year!
B: Congratulations! Though I'd have thought Mint's group stood a better chance.
A: ______
B: No, no — I just meant theirs had more data. Yours was clearly more original.

explanation.en: B's back-handed remark could sound like an insult, and B's last line ('No, no — I just meant…') denies one. So A must have asked 'Are you saying we didn't deserve it?' The other replies do not provoke that denial.
explanation.th: คำพูดของ B ฟังดูเหมือนดูถูกแฝง และประโยคสุดท้าย No, no — I just meant… เป็นการปฏิเสธว่าไม่ได้ตั้งใจ A จึงต้องถามว่า Are you saying we didn't deserve it? ส่วนคำตอบอื่นไม่ทำให้ B ต้องรีบแก้ตัว

choices: Are you saying we didn't deserve it?
Thank you — we worked really hard on it.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความสอดคล้องกับ every one of

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องของประธานและกริยา

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: Every one of the [[students]] [[have]] [[handed in]] the form [[on]] time.

explanation.en: The subject is 'Every one', which is singular, so the verb must be 'has handed in'.
explanation.th: ประธานคือ Every one ซึ่งเป็นเอกพจน์ กริยาจึงต้องเป็น has handed in

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Idiom: turn a blind eye to
skill.th: สำนวน: turn a blind eye to

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วม (collocation)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The minister [[was]] accused [[of]] [[turning]] a blind eye [[on]] corruption within her own department.

explanation.en: The idiom is 'turn a blind eye to' something (pretend not to notice it), not 'on'.
explanation.th: สำนวนคือ turn a blind eye to (แกล้งทำเป็นมองไม่เห็น) ไม่ใช่ on

items.subject: eng

skill.th: despite กับ although

topic.th: คำเชื่อม

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Despite]] she had trained for months, Pim [[failed]] to qualify, [[finishing]] just [[a fraction of]] a second behind.

explanation.en: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a full clause. Before 'she had trained' we need 'Although' (or 'Despite having trained').
explanation.th: Despite ตามด้วยคำนามหรือ V-ing ไม่ใช่ประโยคเต็ม ก่อน she had trained ต้องใช้ Although (หรือ Despite having trained)

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำนามนับไม่ได้: evidence

topic.th: คำนามนับได้และนับไม่ได้

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: Researchers [[have]] [[found]] [[a clear]] evidence that the drug [[reduces]] symptoms in most patients.

explanation.en: 'Evidence' is uncountable and cannot take 'a': 'clear evidence' or 'a clear piece of evidence'.
explanation.th: evidence เป็นนามนับไม่ได้ ใช้ a ไม่ได้ ต้องเป็น clear evidence หรือ a clear piece of evidence

items.subject: eng

skill.th: รูปกริยา: decide + to V

topic.th: รูปกริยา

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: So [[successful]] [[was]] the campaign [[that]] the government decided [[extending]] it to other provinces.

explanation.en: 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive: 'decided to extend it'. The inversion 'So successful was the campaign that…' is correct.
explanation.th: decide ตามด้วย to V จึงเป็น decided to extend it ส่วนการสลับที่ So successful was the campaign that… ถูกต้องแล้ว

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การสลับที่หลัง Only after

topic.th: การสลับที่ประธานกับกริยา (inversion)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: Only after the results [[had been]] published [[the team realised]] [[how]] [[seriously]] the data had been misread.

explanation.en: When a sentence begins with 'Only after + clause', the main clause is inverted: 'did the team realise'.
explanation.th: เมื่อขึ้นต้นด้วย Only after + clause ประโยคหลักต้องสลับที่ เป็น did the team realise

items.subject: eng

skill.th: โครงสร้าง The more …, the more …

topic.th: โครงสร้างประโยค

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[More]] the city [[expands]], the [[harder]] it becomes to [[preserve]] its green spaces.

explanation.en: The double comparative needs 'the' in both halves: 'The more the city expands, the harder it becomes…'.
explanation.th: โครงสร้างเปรียบเทียบคู่ต้องมี the ทั้งสองส่วน: The more the city expands, the harder it becomes…

items.subject: eng

skill.th: collocation: arrive at a conclusion

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วม (collocation)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: After weeks of [[heated]] debate, the panel [[finally]] [[arrived to]] a conclusion [[that]] satisfied neither side.

explanation.en: We 'arrive at' (or 'reach' / 'come to') a conclusion; 'arrive to' is never correct.
explanation.th: ใช้ arrive at (หรือ reach / come to) a conclusion ส่วน arrive to ผิดเสมอ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความสับสนระหว่าง lie / lay

topic.th: รูปกริยา

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Laying]] on the beach all afternoon, he [[failed]] to notice how [[badly]] his shoulders [[were burning]].

explanation.en: 'Lay' needs an object (lay something down). To rest horizontally is 'lie', so the participle is 'Lying on the beach'.
explanation.th: lay ต้องมีกรรม (วางบางสิ่งลง) ส่วนการนอนเอนคือ lie รูป participle จึงเป็น Lying on the beach

items.subject: eng

skill.th: participle รูป passive

topic.th: รูปกริยา

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The documentary [[offers]] a [[rare]] glimpse into the lives of nomadic herders, [[whose]] traditions are [[threatening]] by climate change.

explanation.en: The traditions are endangered by climate change, not doing the threatening, so the passive is needed: 'are threatened by climate change'.
explanation.th: ประเพณีถูกคุกคามโดยการเปลี่ยนแปลงสภาพภูมิอากาศ ไม่ได้เป็นผู้คุกคาม จึงต้องใช้ passive: are threatened by climate change

items.subject: eng

skill.th: กริยา + as: hail as

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความข่าว/สารคดี

items.passage: Cultivated meat — animal cells grown in steel tanks rather than on farms — has been hailed (1) ______ a solution to some of the most pressing problems of our time, from greenhouse gas emissions to animal welfare. Its supporters argue that it could (2) ______ the need to raise and slaughter billions of animals a year. Sceptics, however, point out that the technology remains extremely expensive, and that producing it on an industrial scale would require (3) ______ amounts of energy. There are cultural obstacles, too. Food is bound up with identity, and many consumers are (4) ______ of anything they regard as "unnatural", however safe it may be shown to be. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may therefore depend less on scientific breakthroughs (5) ______ on public perception.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (1)?

explanation.en: The pattern is 'hail something as something' (praise it publicly as): 'hailed as a solution'.
explanation.th: รูปแบบคือ hail something as something (ยกย่องว่าเป็น) จึงเป็น hailed as a solution

items.subject: eng

skill.th: phrasal verb: do away with

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความข่าว/สารคดี

items.passage: Cultivated meat — animal cells grown in steel tanks rather than on farms — has been hailed (1) ______ a solution to some of the most pressing problems of our time, from greenhouse gas emissions to animal welfare. Its supporters argue that it could (2) ______ the need to raise and slaughter billions of animals a year. Sceptics, however, point out that the technology remains extremely expensive, and that producing it on an industrial scale would require (3) ______ amounts of energy. There are cultural obstacles, too. Food is bound up with identity, and many consumers are (4) ______ of anything they regard as "unnatural", however safe it may be shown to be. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may therefore depend less on scientific breakthroughs (5) ______ on public perception.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (2)?

explanation.en: 'Do away with' means remove or abolish, which fits ending 'the need to raise and slaughter' animals. 'Put up with' means tolerate, 'come up with' means think of, and 'make up for' means compensate.
explanation.th: do away with แปลว่ากำจัดหรือยกเลิก เหมาะกับการทำให้ไม่ต้องเลี้ยงและฆ่าสัตว์ ส่วน put up with แปลว่าทน come up with แปลว่าคิดขึ้นมา และ make up for แปลว่าชดเชย

items.subject: eng

skill.th: collocation: vast amounts

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความข่าว/สารคดี

items.passage: Cultivated meat — animal cells grown in steel tanks rather than on farms — has been hailed (1) ______ a solution to some of the most pressing problems of our time, from greenhouse gas emissions to animal welfare. Its supporters argue that it could (2) ______ the need to raise and slaughter billions of animals a year. Sceptics, however, point out that the technology remains extremely expensive, and that producing it on an industrial scale would require (3) ______ amounts of energy. There are cultural obstacles, too. Food is bound up with identity, and many consumers are (4) ______ of anything they regard as "unnatural", however safe it may be shown to be. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may therefore depend less on scientific breakthroughs (5) ______ on public perception.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (3)?

explanation.en: 'Vast amounts' is the natural collocation for a very large quantity. 'Wide', 'tall' and 'broad' describe physical size or range and do not combine with 'amounts'.
explanation.th: vast amounts เป็น collocation ที่ใช้กับปริมาณมหาศาล ส่วน wide, tall และ broad ใช้บอกขนาดหรือความกว้างทางกายภาพ ไม่ใช้กับ amounts

items.subject: eng

skill.th: รูปคำ: adjective + of

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความข่าว/สารคดี

items.passage: Cultivated meat — animal cells grown in steel tanks rather than on farms — has been hailed (1) ______ a solution to some of the most pressing problems of our time, from greenhouse gas emissions to animal welfare. Its supporters argue that it could (2) ______ the need to raise and slaughter billions of animals a year. Sceptics, however, point out that the technology remains extremely expensive, and that producing it on an industrial scale would require (3) ______ amounts of energy. There are cultural obstacles, too. Food is bound up with identity, and many consumers are (4) ______ of anything they regard as "unnatural", however safe it may be shown to be. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may therefore depend less on scientific breakthroughs (5) ______ on public perception.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (4)?

explanation.en: After 'are' and before 'of' we need an adjective: 'distrustful of'. The others are a noun/verb, an adverb and a noun.
explanation.th: หลัง are และก่อน of ต้องใช้ adjective จึงเป็น distrustful of ส่วนตัวเลือกอื่นเป็นคำนาม/กริยา adverb และคำนาม

items.subject: eng

skill.th: โครงสร้างเปรียบเทียบ: less … than

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความข่าว/สารคดี

items.passage: Cultivated meat — animal cells grown in steel tanks rather than on farms — has been hailed (1) ______ a solution to some of the most pressing problems of our time, from greenhouse gas emissions to animal welfare. Its supporters argue that it could (2) ______ the need to raise and slaughter billions of animals a year. Sceptics, however, point out that the technology remains extremely expensive, and that producing it on an industrial scale would require (3) ______ amounts of energy. There are cultural obstacles, too. Food is bound up with identity, and many consumers are (4) ______ of anything they regard as "unnatural", however safe it may be shown to be. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may therefore depend less on scientific breakthroughs (5) ______ on public perception.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (5)?

explanation.en: 'Depend less on X ___ on Y' is a comparative, which must be completed by 'than'.
explanation.th: depend less on X ___ on Y เป็นการเปรียบเทียบขั้นกว่า ต้องใช้ than

items.subject: eng

skill.th: stop + V-ing

topic.th: เติมคำในเรื่องสั้น

items.passage: The house had stood empty for so long that the neighbours had stopped (6) ______ it. So when lights appeared in its windows one October evening, the whole street took notice. The new owner turned out to be an elderly woman who kept (7) ______ herself, rarely leaving the house except to buy bread and, oddly, enormous quantities of string. Rumours multiplied. Some said she was a retired spy; (8) ______ insisted she was a witch. It was not until the spring that the truth came out, when the children of the street, who had been dared to look over her wall, discovered a garden (9) ______ every branch and post was hung with tiny, intricately knotted birds made of string — hundreds of them, swaying in the breeze. Far from (10) ______ the children away, the woman invited them in and showed them how to make their own.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (6)?

explanation.en: The neighbours no longer noticed the house, so 'stopped noticing'. 'Stopped to notice' would mean they paused in order to notice it — the opposite.
explanation.th: เพื่อนบ้านเลิกสังเกตบ้านหลังนั้นแล้ว จึงใช้ stopped noticing ส่วน stopped to notice แปลว่าหยุดเพื่อจะสังเกต ซึ่งความหมายตรงข้าม

items.subject: eng

skill.th: สำนวน: keep to oneself

topic.th: เติมคำในเรื่องสั้น

items.passage: The house had stood empty for so long that the neighbours had stopped (6) ______ it. So when lights appeared in its windows one October evening, the whole street took notice. The new owner turned out to be an elderly woman who kept (7) ______ herself, rarely leaving the house except to buy bread and, oddly, enormous quantities of string. Rumours multiplied. Some said she was a retired spy; (8) ______ insisted she was a witch. It was not until the spring that the truth came out, when the children of the street, who had been dared to look over her wall, discovered a garden (9) ______ every branch and post was hung with tiny, intricately knotted birds made of string — hundreds of them, swaying in the breeze. Far from (10) ______ the children away, the woman invited them in and showed them how to make their own.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (7)?

explanation.en: 'Keep to oneself' means to avoid other people's company, which matches 'rarely leaving the house'.
explanation.th: keep to oneself แปลว่าเก็บตัว ไม่ค่อยสุงสิงกับใคร สอดคล้องกับ rarely leaving the house

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ตัวกำหนด: others / the others / another

topic.th: เติมคำในเรื่องสั้น

items.passage: The house had stood empty for so long that the neighbours had stopped (6) ______ it. So when lights appeared in its windows one October evening, the whole street took notice. The new owner turned out to be an elderly woman who kept (7) ______ herself, rarely leaving the house except to buy bread and, oddly, enormous quantities of string. Rumours multiplied. Some said she was a retired spy; (8) ______ insisted she was a witch. It was not until the spring that the truth came out, when the children of the street, who had been dared to look over her wall, discovered a garden (9) ______ every branch and post was hung with tiny, intricately knotted birds made of string — hundreds of them, swaying in the breeze. Far from (10) ______ the children away, the woman invited them in and showed them how to make their own.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (8)?

explanation.en: 'Some said… ; others insisted…' contrasts two unspecified groups. 'The other' would need a noun or refer to one specific remaining person, 'another' means one more person, and 'other' cannot stand alone as a pronoun.
explanation.th: Some said… ; others insisted… เป็นการเปรียบสองกลุ่มที่ไม่เจาะจง ส่วน the other ต้องมีคำนามตามหรือหมายถึงอีกหนึ่งที่เหลืออยู่ another หมายถึงอีกหนึ่งคน และ other ใช้เป็นคำสรรพนามเดี่ยว ๆ ไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำบุพบท + which

topic.th: เติมคำในเรื่องสั้น

items.passage: The house had stood empty for so long that the neighbours had stopped (6) ______ it. So when lights appeared in its windows one October evening, the whole street took notice. The new owner turned out to be an elderly woman who kept (7) ______ herself, rarely leaving the house except to buy bread and, oddly, enormous quantities of string. Rumours multiplied. Some said she was a retired spy; (8) ______ insisted she was a witch. It was not until the spring that the truth came out, when the children of the street, who had been dared to look over her wall, discovered a garden (9) ______ every branch and post was hung with tiny, intricately knotted birds made of string — hundreds of them, swaying in the breeze. Far from (10) ______ the children away, the woman invited them in and showed them how to make their own.
items.stem: Which option best fills gap (9)?

explanation.en: The clause 'every branch and post was hung with…' is already complete, so it needs 'in which' (= where) to attach to 'a garden'. 'Which' and 'that' would need a missing subject or object, and 'whose' would need a noun directly after it.
explanation.th: ประโยค every branch and post was hung with… สมบูรณ์แล้ว จึงต้องใช้ in which (= where) เชื่อมกับ a garden ส่วน which และ that ต้องมีประธานหรือกรรมที่ขาด และ whose ต้องตามด้วยคำนามทันที

items.passage:
BANGKOK — Tiny fragments of plastic were found in the digestive tracts of more than two-thirds of fish bought from markets along the Gulf of Thailand, according to a study published this week.

Researchers bought 400 fish of twelve common species from markets in four coastal provinces over a period of eighteen months. Particles smaller than five millimetres — mostly fibres from synthetic clothing and fragments of packaging — were detected in 71 per cent of the samples. Species that feed near the sea floor were the most heavily affected.

The lead author, a marine scientist who has studied plastic pollution for more than a decade, was careful to put the findings in context. "We are not telling people to stop eating fish," she said. "Most of the particles were in the gut, which is usually removed before cooking. What concerns us is what these numbers tell us about the state of the sea itself."

Her caution was not shared by all. Within hours of the study's release, several social media accounts had circulated posts warning that seafood was "poisoned", and at least one large coastal market reported a sharp fall in sales the following morning.

Fishing associations reacted angrily, accusing the media of sensationalism. A spokesman pointed out that the study did not measure whether eating such fish posed any risk to human health — a point the researchers themselves acknowledge. "That is the next question," the lead author said, "and it is a much harder one to answer."

Environmental groups, meanwhile, said the study confirmed what they had long argued: that the problem cannot be solved by beach clean-ups alone. They are calling for limits on single-use packaging and for washing machines to be fitted with filters that capture synthetic fibres before they reach the drains.
items.stem: What was the study's main finding?

explanation.en: Particles were found in 71 per cent of the fish. The study did not measure health risk, and the other claims are not made.
explanation.th: พบเศษพลาสติกในปลาร้อยละ 71 การศึกษาไม่ได้วัดความเสี่ยงต่อสุขภาพ และข้ออ้างอื่นไม่มีในข่าว

choices: Most plastic in the sea comes from fishing boats.
Fish sold in markets contain more plastic than fish caught at sea.
Plastic particles were present in most of the fish sampled.
Eating fish from the Gulf of Thailand is dangerous to health.

items.passage:
For forty years my uncle Prasit painted the same view: the river below his house, the temple roof on the far bank, and the hills beyond. He painted it at dawn and at dusk, in the rainy season and in the dry, and he sold almost none of the pictures. They stood stacked against the walls of every room, so that visiting him was like walking through a very slow film of the same afternoon.

The family regarded this as a harmless eccentricity, like his refusal to own a telephone. My mother, his younger sister, described him to strangers as "artistic", in the tone other people use for "unemployed".

When he died, we expected to spend a weekend clearing the house. Instead, a man in a linen suit arrived from a gallery in the capital and asked, very politely, whether he might look at the paintings. He spent four hours with them. Then he asked whether we had noticed the temple.

We had not. Looking again, in the order he arranged them, we saw what forty years of glances had missed. In the earliest paintings the temple roof was bright and whole. Over the years it faded, cracked and sagged; in some of the later canvases it had all but disappeared behind the scaffolding of a new hotel. And then — in the final picture, finished a week before my uncle died — the hotel was gone, and the temple stood as it had in the first painting, golden and entire.

"The hotel is still there," my mother said quietly. "I drove past it this morning."

The man in the linen suit nodded. "Yes," he said. "I don't think he was painting what he saw."

The exhibition opens next month. My mother has been to the gallery twice to help with the labels, and she has stopped saying "artistic" in that particular tone.

explanation.en: The text says the family 'regarded this as a harmless eccentricity'. He sold almost none of the paintings, so it was not a business.

As a talent that would one day make him famous

For forty years my uncle Prasit painted the same view: the river below his house, the temple roof on the far bank, and the hills beyond. He painted it at dawn and at dusk, in the rainy season and in the dry, and he sold almost none of the pictures. They stood stacked against the walls of every room, so that visiting him was like walking through a very slow film of the same afternoon.

The family regarded this as a harmless eccentricity, like his refusal to own a telephone. My mother, his younger sister, described him to strangers as "artistic", in the tone other people use for "unemployed".

When he died, we expected to spend a weekend clearing the house. Instead, a man in a linen suit arrived from a gallery in the capital and asked, very politely, whether he might look at the paintings. He spent four hours with them. Then he asked whether we had noticed the temple.

We had not. Looking again, in the order he arranged them, we saw what forty years of glances had missed. In the earliest paintings the temple roof was bright and whole. Over the years it faded, cracked and sagged; in some of the later canvases it had all but disappeared behind the scaffolding of a new hotel. And then — in the final picture, finished a week before my uncle died — the hotel was gone, and the temple stood as it had in the first painting, golden and entire.

"The hotel is still there," my mother said quietly. "I drove past it this morning."

The man in the linen suit nodded. "Yes," he said. "I don't think he was painting what he saw."

The exhibition opens next month. My mother has been to the gallery twice to help with the labels, and she has stopped saying "artistic" in that particular tone.

The new Central Library has been open for six weeks, and it has already appeared in three international design magazines. It is not hard to see why. The building is a gleaming curve of glass and white concrete that seems to float above the plaza, and at night, lit from within, it looks less like a library than a lantern someone has set down gently on the city. Photographers adore it.

Readers may be less enthusiastic. The main reading room, the building's centrepiece, is a vast, echoing space with a ceiling four storeys high. It is magnificent to stand in and almost impossible to concentrate in: every footstep, every whispered conversation, every chair scraped across the stone floor carries to the far corners. On both of my visits, the most crowded area of the building was not the reading room at all but a narrow, carpeted corridor on the second floor, where students sat on the floor with their backs against the wall because it was the only quiet place they could find.

The books themselves seem almost an afterthought. Large parts of the collection have been moved to an off-site store and must be ordered two days in advance; the shelves that remain have been arranged, apparently, for visual effect, with the result that the children's section is on the top floor, reached by a staircase that no parent with a pushchair will enjoy.

None of this is to say the building is a failure. As a civic symbol it is undeniably powerful, and the plaza outside has quickly become a popular place to meet. But a library is not only a symbol. It is a place where people need to sit, think and find things, and on those modest measures the Central Library has some way to go. Perhaps its next prize could be for acoustics.

explanation.en: The review praises the look of the building but criticises noise, hidden books and an awkward layout — all practical problems for readers. The plaza is called popular, and the press attention is real.

items.passage:
Every few months, an article appears listing the "untranslatable words" of the world's languages: the Portuguese saudade, the Japanese wabi-sabi, the Thai kreng jai. Such lists are charming, and they usually come with the suggestion that each word opens a window onto a unique national soul. The Danes, we are told, are happier because they have hygge.

Linguists tend to be more sceptical. For one thing, almost any word can be translated if one is willing to use a phrase rather than a single word. Kreng jai may have no exact English equivalent, but its meaning — a reluctance to impose on others, out of consideration for their feelings — can be explained perfectly well in a sentence. What is lost is not the idea but the convenience of having it packed into a single, familiar word.

For another, the claim that a language determines what its speakers are able to think has a long and troubled history. In its strongest form, it suggests that speakers of a language without a word for something cannot grasp the concept at all — an idea the evidence has largely failed to support. English speakers have no trouble recognising the feeling the Germans call Schadenfreude; they have simply had to borrow the word.

Yet the sceptics can be too dismissive. There is good evidence that language influences, in subtler ways, what we notice and remember. Speakers of languages that require them to mark whether information was seen directly or merely heard about, for example, may pay closer attention to the source of what they know. A word does not create a feeling, but having one may make it easier to recognise, to discuss and, perhaps, to value.

The truth, then, is less romantic than the lists suggest, but more interesting. Languages do not lock us inside separate worlds. They simply light some corners of the shared one more brightly than others.

items.passage:
Every few months, an article appears listing the "untranslatable words" of the world's languages: the Portuguese saudade, the Japanese wabi-sabi, the Thai kreng jai. Such lists are charming, and they usually come with the suggestion that each word opens a window onto a unique national soul. The Danes, we are told, are happier because they have hygge.

Linguists tend to be more sceptical. For one thing, almost any word can be translated if one is willing to use a phrase rather than a single word. Kreng jai may have no exact English equivalent, but its meaning — a reluctance to impose on others, out of consideration for their feelings — can be explained perfectly well in a sentence. What is lost is not the idea but the convenience of having it packed into a single, familiar word.

For another, the claim that a language determines what its speakers are able to think has a long and troubled history. In its strongest form, it suggests that speakers of a language without a word for something cannot grasp the concept at all — an idea the evidence has largely failed to support. English speakers have no trouble recognising the feeling the Germans call Schadenfreude; they have simply had to borrow the word.

Yet the sceptics can be too dismissive. There is good evidence that language influences, in subtler ways, what we notice and remember. Speakers of languages that require them to mark whether information was seen directly or merely heard about, for example, may pay closer attention to the source of what they know. A word does not create a feeling, but having one may make it easier to recognise, to discuss and, perhaps, to value.

The truth, then, is less romantic than the lists suggest, but more interesting. Languages do not lock us inside separate worlds. They simply light some corners of the shared one more brightly than others.
items.stem: "They simply light some corners of the shared one more brightly than others." What does this metaphor suggest?

explanation.en: 'The shared one' is the one world we all live in. Languages do not separate us into different worlds; they just draw more attention to some aspects of it.
